The club was formed on 25 January 1890, making it Spain's second oldest sporting club solely devoted to football, after [[Recreativo de Huelva]].{{cite web |date=9 October 2012 |title=The day Spanish football was born |url=http://www.marca.com/2012/09/10/en/football/spanish_football/1347305537.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150206222215/http://www.marca.com/2012/09/10/en/football/spanish_football/1347305537.html |archive-date=6 February 2015 |access-date=6 February 2015 |publisher=Marca}}{{cite web |date=11 October 2012 |title=How Glasgow man Hugh McColl helped set up Spain's oldest football club |url=http://www.eveningtimes.co.uk/news/how-glasgow-man-hugh-mccoll-helped-set-up-spains-oldest-football-club-104007n.19098806 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150217011754/http://www.eveningtimes.co.uk/news/how-glasgow-man-hugh-mccoll-helped-set-up-spains-oldest-football-club-104007n.19098806 |archive-date=17 February 2015 |access-date=6 February 2015 |work=Evening Times}}{{Cite web |title=Scottish Influence on Spanish Football |url=https://www.scottishfootballmuseum.org.uk/news/scottish-influence-on-spanish-football/ |access-date=2025-04-05 |website=Scottish Football Museum |language=en}} The Scottish-born [[Edward F. Johnston|Edward Farquharson Johnston]] was one of Sevilla's founders, also becoming their first president. On 14 October 1905, the club's articles of association were registered in the Civil Government of Seville under the presidency of the Jerez-born José Luis Gallegos Arnosa. Sevilla are also the most successful football club in [[Andalusia]] in terms of titles, with eighteen Andalusian Cups,{{cite web|title=Honours|url=https://sevillafc.es/en/the-club/honours|access-date=2022-01-03|website=sevillafc.es|archive-date=6 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211106153022/https://sevillafc.es/en/the-club/honours|url-status=live}} one [[La Liga]] title in [[1945–46 La Liga|1945–46]], five [[Copa del Rey|Spanish Cup]] titles ([[1935 Copa del Presidente de la República|1935]], [[1939 Copa del Generalísimo|1939]], [[1947–48 Copa del Generalísimo|1948]], [[2006–07 Copa del Rey|2007]] and [[2009–10 Copa del Rey|2010]]), one [[Supercopa de España|Spanish Super Cup]] ([[2007 Supercopa de España|2007]]), a [[List of UEFA club competition winners|record]] seven [[UEFA Europa League|UEFA Cups / UEFA Europa Leagues]] ([[2005–06 UEFA Cup|2006]], [[2006–07 UEFA Cup|2007]], [[2013–14 UEFA Europa League|2014]], [[2014–15 UEFA Europa League|2015]], [[2015–16 UEFA Europa League|2016]], [[2019–20 UEFA Europa League|2020]], and [[2022–23 UEFA Europa League|2023]]) and one [[UEFA Super Cup]] ([[2006 UEFA Super Cup|2006]]). They were also designated by the [[International Federation of Football History & Statistics]] as the [[IFFHS World's Best Club|World's Best Club]] in 2006 and 2007, thus being the first club to achieve this distinction in two consecutive years. The reserve team [[Sevilla Atlético]], founded in 1958, currently play in {{Spanish football updater|Sevilla Atlético}}. Other clubs related to Sevilla FC include their women's team. The rowing team that defends its crest in the yearly Sevilla-Betis [[Boat racing|boat race]] is not a section of the club but a call-up of registered-as-supporters professional rowers from the various rowing clubs of Seville. The club's home ground is the 43,883-seat [[Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán Stadium]]. It is located in the neighborhood of [[Nervión, Seville]], and is named after [[Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán]], who was the president of Sevilla for 17 years. Sevilla has a long-standing rivalry with cross-city rival [[Real Betis]], and matches between the pair are the [[Seville derby]]. ==History== ===Foundation to Civil War=== The practice of football was introduced in Seville at the end of the 19th century by the large British expatriate population in the city, composed by owners or managers of manufacturing companies based in the capital of [[Andalusia]]. '''Sevilla Fútbol Club''' was founded on [[Burns Night]] 25 January 1890 as ''Sevilla Foot-ball Club'' (in English).{{cite web |date=5 October 2012 |title=Your BNA Stories: Sevilla Football Club – the Oldest Football Club in Spain, Founded in 1905 by British Residents |url=http://blog.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/your-bna-stories-sevilla-football-club-the-oldest-football-club-in-spain-founded-in-1890-by-british-residents/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131007001907/http://blog.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/your-bna-stories-sevilla-football-club-the-oldest-football-club-in-spain-founded-in-1890-by-british-residents/ |archive-date=7 October 2013 |access-date=5 October 2013 |publisher=The British Newspaper Archive}}{{cite web |date=7 February 2013 |title=Courier proves Seville's claim as Spain's oldest football club |url=http://www.thecourier.co.uk/news/local/dundee/courier-proves-seville-s-claim-as-spain-s-oldest-football-club-1.67812 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130213145810/http://www.thecourier.co.uk/news/local/dundee/courier-proves-seville-s-claim-as-spain-s-oldest-football-club-1.67812 |archive-date=13 February 2013 |publisher=The Courier}}{{cite book |author = Juan Castro y Agustín Rodríguez |title = Breve Historia del Sevilla F. C. «Historia (1890 a 1914)»] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150129005725/http://www.sevillafc.es/nuevaweb/el_club/historia |date=29 January 2015 }}{{Excessive citations inline|date=March 2025}} Sevilla FC was duly formed on 25 January 1890 while a group of young British, mainly Scots, along with other young men of Spanish origin, celebrated [[Burns supper|Burns Night]] in Seville.{{cite web |url=https://www.scottishfa.co.uk/news/sevilla-fc-commemorate-scottish-roots/?rid=14258 |title=Sevilla FC commemorate Scottish roots |publisher=Scottish Football Association |date=7 June 2018 |access-date=7 June 2018 |archive-date=12 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612210443/https://www.scottishfa.co.uk/news/sevilla-fc-commemorate-scottish-roots/?rid=14258 |url-status=live }} The club's founding document, published on the ''[[Dundee Courier]]'''s edition of 17 March 1890 describes in full detail the formation of the club and how those young founding members decided first to play under Association Rules, secondly to bear the word "football" within its name and thirdly, to elect their "office-bearers". The following paragraph is an extract of that article: {{blockquote|Some six weeks ago a few enthusiastic young residents of British origin met in one of the cafés for the purpose of considering a proposal that we should start an Athletic Association, the want of exercise being greatly felt by the majority of us, who are chiefly engaged in mercantile pursuits. After a deal of talk and limited consumption of small beer, the "Club de Football de Sevilla" was duly formed and office-bearers elected. It was decided we should play Association rules (...) We were about half and half Spanish and British}}[[File:Edward_Farquharson_Johnston.png|alt=|thumb|[[Edward F. Johnston]], founder, and the first President|200x200px]]The club's first president was the Scot Mr. [[Edward F. Johnston|Edward Farquharson Johnston]] (Elgin, 14 October 1854), who was the British vice-consul in Seville and co-proprietor of the firm MacAndrews & Co., ship-owners with commercial lines between Spain and the UK, one of them being the transport of [[Seville orange]]s. [[Hugh MacColl (footballer)|Hugh MacColl]], another Scottish young man (Glasgow, 9 June 1861), a marine engineer who at that time had moved to Seville to work as the technical manager of Portilla White foundry, was their first captain. One of Maccoll's partners in the Portilla White foundry in Seville, Isaias White junior, was the club's first secretary. He was the son of an English entrepreneur who founded the aforesaid company, one of the major foundries in Spain at the end of the 19th century. To celebrate the foundation of the club, [[Isaias White]] sent a letter to Huelva Recreation Club, to invite them to play a football match in Seville. That letter was published by the Spanish newspaper ''La Provincia''. The Huelva club accepted the invitation and the match took place on 8 March 1890, being thus the [[First football match in Spain|first official match ever played in Spain]].{{cite web |url=https://www.marca.com/2012/09/10/en/football/spanish_football/1347305537.html |title=The day Spanish football was born – MARCA.com (English version) |publisher=MARCA.com |date= |accessdate=2022-02-08 |archive-date=9 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211109153345/https://www.marca.com/2012/09/10/en/football/spanish_football/1347305537.html |url-status=live }} Sevilla FC won that historical match 2–0, with the first goal in an official match in Spanish football history scored by the Seville team player Ritson. Isaias lived at Calle Bailen 41{{cite web|title=La calle Bailén|date=5 May 2010|url=http://sevillistasoy.blogspot.co.uk/2010/05/la-calle-bailen.html|access-date=16 November 2015|archive-date=17 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117014618/http://sevillistasoy.blogspot.co.uk/2010/05/la-calle-bailen.html|url-status=live}} in Seville (the house still exists but has since been renumbered) making this the first home of Sevilla FC. In 1907, Sevilla Balompíe was founded, followed by Betis Football Club in 1909, Recreativo de Sevilla and Español de Sevilla. More clubs were formed as the years passed and more competitive matches were organized between the teams, although Sevilla FC, the oldest club of the city, imposed its supremacy over the other clubs in this early period. [[File:Sevilla_Fútbol_Club_-_Real_Club_Recreativo_de_Huelva_(1909).jpg|alt=|thumb|Sevilla Fútbol Club – Real Club Recreativo de Huelva (1909)|267x267px]]In 1912, the first Copa de Sevilla was played and won by Sevilla FC. From 1915 to 1940, the [[Campeonato Regional Sur]] (also known as the Copa Andalucía) was organized by the "Federación Sur" ([[Royal Andalusian Football Federation|Andalusian FA]]) and these championships included Sevilla FC, Real Betis Balompié, Recreativo de Huelva, Español de Cádiz and the sporadic participation of other clubs such as Nacional de Sevilla and Córdoba. The domination of Sevilla was so evident that of the 20 championships played, 17 were won by Sevilla FC, (the three remaining being won by Español de de Cádiz, Recreativo de Huelva and Real Betis Balompié). In 1917, Sevilla FC participated in the "Copa de España" for the first time and became the first Andalusian team to reach the final round of the competition. In 1928, when the "Campeonato Nacional de Liga" (National League Championships) was organized, Sevilla FC was not part of the First Division due to their defeat to [[Racing de Santander]] in an elimination game that was set up to decide which of the two teams would compete in the newly formed league. At the end of the 1933–34 season, Sevilla FC was promoted to the First Division of the "Campeonato Nacional de Liga." In 1935, they were proclaimed "Campeón de Copa" (Cup Champions) for the first time by defeating [[CE Sabadell FC|Sabadell]], repeated in 1939 against [[Racing de Ferrol]] and again in 1948 against [[Celta de Vigo]]. The club participated in two other finals, but conceded defeat to [[Athletic Bilbao]] in 1955 and to [[Real Madrid C.F.|Real Madrid]] in 1962. Sevilla FC remained in the First Division from the 1933–34 season until 1968, when they were relegated to the Second Division, a tier from which they have never further been relegated from. [[File:Priemrescudodelsevilla2.JPG|thumb|Sevilla's first crest, displayed on a former player's shirt in the club museum]] The 1945–46 season was one of high importance in the history of Sevilla, as it marked the first, and to date only, time in which Sevilla FC were League champions. On four other occasions, the club was proclaimed "subcampeón de Liga" (League Runner-up: 1939–40, 1942–43, 1950–51 and 1956–57). Including the 2021–22 season, Sevilla has participated 78 times in the First Division and 13 in the Second Division, never dropping below the Second Division. Sevilla has also participated in four European tournaments, the "Copa de Europa" (European League Winners Cup) (1957–58); Recopa (Winners Cup) (1962–63) and [[UEFA Europa League|UEFA Cup]] on nine occasions (1966–67, 1970–71, 1982–83, 1983–84, 1990–91, 1995–96, 2004–05, 2005–06 and 2006–07). Sevilla also participated in the [[UEFA Champions League]] in [[2007–08 UEFA Champions League|2007–08]]. There are more than 400 individuals who currently play for the Sevilla FC organization, which includes two semi-professional teams (in Second Division A – second national category) and 12 youth teams.[[File:Balondefutbol1924.JPG|thumb|Club ball in the museum]] Sevilla has always counted on having international players within its ranks to aid in the pursuit of trophies. The first of these players were Spencer and Herminio in the 1920s. Juan Arza, an international player from the 1940s, was proclaimed top scorer of the Spanish League in the 1954–55 season, with 29 goals. About 30 Sevilla players have been chosen to play for the [[Spain men's national football team|Spain national football team]] over the years. Foreign players have always played an integral part in the success of Sevilla FC with Diego Maradona representing the most well known among them during his spell with the club during the 1992–93 season. During the same season, Sevilla FC was managed by Carlos Salvador Bilardo, a world champion manager. Historically, Sevilla FC has fielded teams in a variety of other sports including: basketball, rugby, rowing, athletics, and [[Olympic weightlifting|weightlifting]] or petanca. Presently, Sevilla FC counts twenty-five professional teams on its ledgers (one of these being in the second national category) and a women's football team in the Honor Division. Sevilla FC's stadium, the [[Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán Stadium|Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán]], was inaugurated in 1958 and is one of the largest stadiums in Spain, and has the honor of hosting a World Cup semi-final match in [[1982 FIFA World Cup|1982]]. After its final completion, the stadium had a maximum capacity of 75,000 spectators, but since its latest remodelling, the stadium has been converted to an all-seat with a covering added to the main seating area, reducing the capacity to its current count of 45,000 spectators. ===First successes=== [[File:Suscripcionpopularnuevoestadio.JPG|thumb|Bond issue to build the new stadium (1957)]] [[File:Bustoderamonsanchezpizjuan2.JPG|thumb|upright|Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán's bust placed at the stadium]] Sevilla had their first spell of national success in the decade following the end of the Civil War, winning the [[1945–46 La Liga]] title and two [[Copa del Rey]] titles. In the first season of this (1939–40), Sevilla won the cup on 25 June, beating Racing de Ferrol 6–2 in [[Barcelona]].{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tabless/spancuphist.html |title=Spain – List of Cup Finals |website=[[RSSSF]] |access-date=2 October 2021 |archive-date=31 July 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170731071239/http://www.rsssf.com/tabless/spancuphist.html |url-status=live }} That same season, the side lost the Liga title on the last day to [[Atlético Madrid]] after drawing 3–3 against [[Hércules CF|Hércules]].{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tabless/spanhist3949.html |title=Spain, Final Tables 1939–1949 |website=[[RSSSF]] |access-date=2 October 2021 |archive-date=3 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220803104223/https://www.rsssf.org/tabless/spanhist3949.html |url-status=live }} The Sevilla forward line was known as ''los stukas'' after the [[Junkers Ju 87|German bomber aircraft]], and scored 216 goals over four seasons. It comprised López, Torrontegui, [[Campanal I|Campanal]], Raimundo, Berrocal and [[Pepillo (footballer, born 1916)|Pepillo]]. {{cite web |url = http://www.sevillafc.es/_www/club.php?op=his5 |title = Historia del Sevilla 1939–1945 |publisher = Web oficial del Sevilla F. C. |access-date = 31 July 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091214042620/http://www.sevillafc.es//_www/club.php?op=his5 |archive-date = 14 December 2009}} In 1941, President [[Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán]] left the club to manage the [[Royal Spanish Football Federation|Spanish Football Federation]]. After his departure, Antonio Sánchez Ramos occupied temporarily occupied the position until the permanent appointment of [[Jerónimo Pérez de Vargas|Jerónimo Domínguez y Pérez de Vargas, Marquess of Contadero]], who was president of the club for six years until the return of Sánchez Pizjuán.{{cite web |url = http://www.abc.es/informacion/futbolsevilla/sevilla/historia/sigue2.asp |title = Historia del Sevilla (1939–1948) |publisher = [[ABC (España)|ABC]] |access-date = 31 July 2010 |archive-date = 18 July 2011 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110718113755/http://www.abc.es/informacion/futbolsevilla/sevilla/historia/sigue2.asp |url-status = live }} Sevilla was runner-up to Athletic Bilbao in the 1942–43 season and came third a season later. Sevilla won its only Liga title in 1945–46, edging [[FC Barcelona]] by one point.{{cite web |url = http://www.sevillafc.es/_www/club.php?op=his6 |title = Campeón de Liga 1945/46 |publisher = sevillafc.es.Historia |access-date = 13 August 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091214042643/http://www.sevillafc.es//_www/club.php?op=his6 |archive-date = 14 December 2009}} Two years later, Sevilla won the [[1948 Copa del Rey]] after beating Celta de Vigo 4–1 in [[Madrid]] on 4 July. The most significant signing of those years was the Spanish international striker [[Juan Arza]]. There was also the debut of the Campanal's nephew, defender Campanal II, with his uncle as a trainer. During the 1950–51 season, with Campanal acting as the coach, the team finished runner-up in La Liga, two points behind Atlético Madrid.{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tabless/spanhist4959.html |title=Spain, Final Tables 1949–1959 |website=[[RSSSF]] |access-date=2 October 2021 |archive-date=3 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220803104226/https://www.rsssf.org/tabless/spanhist4959.html |url-status=live }} Before the 1953–54 season, Argentinean coach [[Helenio Herrera]] was hired. During his time in charge, the club came fifth in the 1953–54 season, fourth in both 1954–55 and 1955–56 and second to Real Madrid in 1956–57. In 1954, the club put the construction of the new stadium out to tender because Nervión Stadium was becoming too small for the club's fanbase. In the 1954–55 season, Arza won the [[Pichichi Trophy]] as La Liga's top scorer, with 28 goals,{{cite web |url = http://www.cosasdefutbol.es/historia-trofeo-pichichi-liga/ |title = Historia: Trofeo Pichichi de la Liga |date = 13 November 2009 |publisher = cosasdefutbol.es |access-date = 13 August 2010 |archive-date = 23 July 2010 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100723213440/http://www.cosasdefutbol.es/historia-trofeo-pichichi-liga/ |url-status = live }} and the team was runner-up in the Copa del Rey. In 1955, for the club's 50th anniversary, a triangular tournament was organized against the French club [[Stade de Reims]] and the Swedish club [[IFK Norrköping]]; Sevilla won. On 28 October 1956, President Sánchez Pizjuán suddenly died. As an appreciation to the deceased leader under whose chairmanship Sevilla had won three Copas del Rey, the fans decided that the club's planned new stadium was to be named in his honour.{{cite web |url=http://www.estadiodeportivo.com/sevilla.php?id=7630 |title=Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán será recordado con un busto |work=Estadio Deportivo |date=12 October 2009 |access-date=11 November 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728114950/http://www.estadiodeportivo.com/sevilla.php?id=7630 |archive-date=28 July 2011}} In the 1956–57 season, the team were Liga runners-up behind Real Madrid, ensuring qualification for the first time to the [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]]. Herrera left the club at the end of the season.{{cite web |url = http://www.sevillafc.es/_www/club.php?op=his9 |title = Historia del Sevilla 1955/1959 |publisher = Web Oficial del Sevilla F. C. |access-date = 31 July 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091214042814/http://www.sevillafc.es//_www/club.php?op=his9 |archive-date = 14 December 2009}} The club needed a victory on the final day of the next season to avoid relegation but reached the round of 8 of the European Cup before being knocked out by holders and eventual champions Real Madrid. After the death of the President, {{Interlanguage link|Ramón de Carranza Gómez|ES}} assumed the position for four years. It is said that he spoke these words at Sánchez Pizjuán's tomb: ''"Dear Ramón, now your friends, among who I am honored to be one, is going to give you Christian burial, and on the following day, giving your body to the ground, we will start working and your dream that the Sevilla FC has a grand stadium will become a reality. Ramón, go in peace to heaven because your wishes will be fulfilled."'' Being true to his words, Carranza made obligation bonds amounting to 50 million pesetas, and a month and a half after Sánchez Pizjuán's death, the first stone in the stadium's construction was placed. The architect was Manuel Muñoz Monasterio, co-designer of the recently built [[Santiago Bernabéu Stadium]], the home of Real Madrid. The [[Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán Stadium]] was ultimately opened on 7 September 1958 as Sevilla played an inaugural friendly against fellow Andalusian club [[Real Jaén]]. The stadium's first official match was on the opening day of the [[1958–59 La Liga|1958–59 season]], where Sevilla beat cross-city Real Betis 4–2.{{cite web |url = http://www.abc.es/informacion/futbolsevilla/sevilla/historia/sigue3.asp |title = Historia del Sevilla F. C. |work = [[ABC (Spain)|ABC]] |access-date = 20 July 2010 |archive-date = 18 July 2011 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110718113737/http://www.abc.es/informacion/futbolsevilla/sevilla/historia/sigue3.asp |url-status = live }} ===Crisis and stability=== [[File:En el Sánchez Pizjuan el 15-11-1961.jpg|thumb|upright|Campanal clearing a ball in the Sánchez Pizjuán Stadium on 15 November 1961]] In the 1970s, Sevilla was forced into selling its top players to pay off debts incurred from the construction of its new stadium; [[Manuel Ruiz Sosa]] transferred to Atlético Madrid, [[Gallego (footballer)|Gallego]] to Barcelona and Juan Batista Agüero to Real Madrid. Moreover, part of the adjacent land to the stadium was also sold to a bank. In the [[1967–68 La Liga|1967–68 season]], Sevilla returned to the Second Division for the first time in 31 years but was promoted back after one season. The next season, Austrian coach [[Max Merkel]], nicknamed "Mr. Whip" for his usage of severe and harsh discipline techniques and training, was hired.{{cite web |url=http://archivo.lavozdeasturias.es/html/309635.html |title=Muere Max Merkel, 'Míster Látigo' |access-date=11 November 2010 |author=La Voz de Asturias |date=30 November 2006 |work=Público |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718081944/http://archivo.lavozdeasturias.es/html/309635.html |archive-date=18 July 2011}} That season, the club finished third in the league. However, the club was relegated again at the end of the [[1972–73 La Liga|1972–73 season]]. In 1973, Sevilla signed their first-ever black player, Gambian winger [[Biri Biri]], from the Danish club [[Boldklubben 1901]]. He remained at the club until 1978 and became a cult figure, with an [[ultras|ultra group]] named after him surviving to this day. In the [[1974–75 La Liga|1974–75 season]], with the Argentine [[Roque Olsen]] in charge, the club returned to the First Division. In the late 1970s, Sevilla signed Argentinians such as [[Héctor Scotta]] and [[Daniel Bertoni]].{{cite web |url = http://www.abc.es/informacion/futbolsevilla/sevilla/historia/sigue3.asp |title = Historia del Sevilla F. C. (1921–1939) |editor = [[ABC (España)|ABC]] |access-date = 20 July 2010 |archive-date = 18 July 2011 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110718113737/http://www.abc.es/informacion/futbolsevilla/sevilla/historia/sigue3.asp |url-status = live }}{{cite web |url = http://www.sevillafc.es/_www/club.php?op=his13 |title = Historia del Sevilla (1971–1995) |publisher = Web oficial del Sevilla F. C. |access-date = 31 July 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091212231315/http://sevillafc.es/_www/club.php?op=his13 |archive-date = 12 December 2009}} Directed first by Miguel Muñoz and later by Manolo Cardo, the team participated in two consecutive seasons of the UEFA Cup from 1981 to 1983. The 75th anniversary of the club was celebrated with a variety of social events and a match against the Brazilian side [[Santos FC|Santos]]. In 1982, the [[1982 FIFA World Cup|World Cup]] was held in Spain and Sevilla's Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán was the venue for the semi-final match between [[West Germany national football team|West Germany]] and [[France national football team|France]].{{cite book |last = Basse |first = Pierre-Louis |publisher = Privé |title = Séville 82 |year = 2005 |isbn = 2-35076-003-0 |language = fr}} In 1984, Eugenio Montes Cabeza finished his 11-year presidency and was replaced by the cattle businessman Gabriel Rojas, who as the vice-president had made several advancements to the club's stadium. In the [[1985–86 La Liga|1985–86 season]], Manolo Cardo left his management position after five years in charge, while [[Francisco López Alfaro|Francisco]] played in the [[1986 FIFA World Cup]] for Spain. [[Vicente Cantatore]] led the club to UEFA Cup qualification at the end of the [[1989–90 La Liga|1989–90 season]], with Austrian forward [[Toni Polster]] scoring a club-record 33 Liga goals.{{cite web |url = http://www.abc.es/informacion/futbolsevilla/sevilla/historia/sigue5.asp |title = Historia del Sevilla (1983–1991) |publisher = [[ABC (España)|ABC]] |access-date = 31 July 2010 |archive-date = 18 July 2011 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110718113803/http://www.abc.es/informacion/futbolsevilla/sevilla/historia/sigue5.asp |url-status = live }} In the [[1992–93 La Liga|1992–93 season]], after several months of negotiations, world-renowned Argentine [[Diego Maradona]] signed from [[S.S.C. Napoli|Napoli]] for a fee of $7.5 million. His time at the club, however, was unsuccessful, and he was released in large part due to his periodic injuries and clashes with coach Bilardo.{{cite web |url=http://edant.clarin.com/diario/especiales/maradona/nota1.htm |title=El Mejor amigo de la pelota |publisher=edant.clarin.com |access-date=3 December 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110916174958/http://edant.clarin.com/diario/especiales/maradona/nota1.htm |archive-date=16 September 2011 |url-status=dead}} In the following seasons, [[Luis Aragonés]] became manager and finished the [[1994–95 La Liga|1994–95 season]] with qualification to next season's UEFA Cup. At the end of the 1994–95 season, despite the pleas of the club's directors, Sevilla, along with Celta de Vigo, were one of two clubs relegated from the top flight on reasons of administration, provoking action from fans. The action resulted in both Sevilla and Celta being reinstated to La Liga.{{cite web |url= http://www.elcorreoweb.es/deportes/sevillafc/100386/quince/anos/descenso/administrativo/sevilla |title= Se cumplen quince años del descenso administrativo del Sevilla |author= Basilio García |date= 1 August 2010 |publisher= Periódico El Correo de Anadalucía.es |access-date= 30 October 2010 |archive-date= 13 February 2013 |archive-url= https://archive.today/20130213060458/http://www.elcorreoweb.es/deportes/sevillafc/100386/quince/anos/descenso/administrativo/sevilla |url-status= live }} These events led to an institutional instability, with the season seeing four presidents and three managers take charge. Sevilla was relegated at the end of the [[1996–97 La Liga|1996–97 season]], after 22 years stayed in top division, but returned in 1999.{{cite web |url = http://www.sevillafc.es/_www/club.php?op=his19 |title = Historia del Sevilla (1995–1999) |publisher = Web oficial del Sevilla F. C. |access-date = 31 July 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091214043257/http://www.sevillafc.es//_www/club.php?op=his19 |archive-date = 14 December 2009}} At the beginning of the 21st century, the presidency of the club was assumed by the popular Roberto Alés.{{cite book |author = Juan Castro y Agustín Rodríguez |title = Breve Historia del Sevilla F. C. Capítulo 39, 2000, llegó el hombre del cosenso. Página 195. |year = 2010 |publisher = Punto Rojo Libros S. L. |id = D.L SE-3847-2010 }} The situation of the club was very delicate at the time; the team had dropped back to the Second Division in 2000 and the squad was weakened by player retirements and the sales of key players. The club opted for a relatively unknown trainer, [[Joaquín Caparrós]], who helped the team win the Second Division with three matches to spare in just his first season at the helm.{{cite web |url = http://www.sevillafc.es/_www/club.php?op=his20 |title = Historia del Sevilla 1999/2003 |publisher = Web oficial del Sevilla F. C. |access-date = 31 July 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091214043324/http://www.sevillafc.es//_www/club.php?op=his20 |archive-date = 14 December 2009}} ===Successes in the 21st century=== In May 2002, Roberto Alés resigned as president, and the Sevillian lawyer José María del Nido assumed the presidency. One of his first decisions was to confirm Caparrós as a coach and [[Monchi]] as sporting director. [[File:Sevilla UEFA Cup 2006.jpg|thumb|Players and staff of Sevilla celebrating the [[2006 UEFA Cup Final|UEFA Cup victory in 2006]]]] On 6 October 2002, before a [[Seville derby]] against Betis at the Sánchez Pizjuán, four Sevilla fans, including a minor, assaulted a security guard. The attack was punished by Sevilla being forced to play their next four home matches behind closed doors, the longest term ever given to a La Liga side. The club finished sixth in the [[2003–04 La Liga]], giving the club qualification for the [[2004–05 UEFA Cup]] and marking a return to continental competition for the first time since the 1995–96 season. In the [[2004–05 La Liga|2004–05]] league season, Sevilla finished sixth and qualified for the [[2005–06 UEFA Cup|following season's UEFA Cup]], entering the competition in the third qualifying round.{{cite web|date=1 June 2006|title=2005/06: Un título 58 años después|url=https://es.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/news/01b6-0e6d8c7b705c-0251c30374c7-1000--2005-06-un-titulo-58-anos-despues/?iv=true|access-date=13 August 2010|publisher=UEFA|archive-date=3 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220103034007/https://es.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/news/01b6-0e6d8c7b705c-0251c30374c7-1000--2005-06-un-titulo-58-anos-despues/?iv=true|url-status=live}} This set up Sevilla's first-ever European triumph in the [[2006 UEFA Cup Final]] at the [[Philips Stadion]] in [[Eindhoven]] on 10 May 2006. The club defeated English club [[Middlesbrough F.C.|Middlesbrough]] 4–0 under new manager [[Juande Ramos]], with the scoring opened by Brazilian striker [[Luís Fabiano]]. In the second-half, Italian substitute [[Enzo Maresca]] scored twice to be named Man of the Match, and Malian striker [[Frédéric Kanouté]] finished the scoring, to give the club its first major title in 58 years on the season of its centenary, which was celebrated in October 2005. Sevilla opened their [[2006–07 La Liga|2006–07 season]] by winning the [[2006 UEFA Super Cup]] on 25 August 2006 with a 3–0 victory over Champions League winners and compatriots Barcelona at the [[Stade Louis II]] in Monaco. The goals were scored by [[Renato (footballer, born 1979)|Renato]], Kanouté and a late penalty by Maresca.{{cite web |url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ySxeBl0C9g8 |title = Supercopa de Europa 2006 F. C. BARCELONA VS SEVILLA F. C. RESUMEN (CADENA SER) PARTE 1 |date = 4 August 2009 |publisher = YouTube |access-date = 13 August 2010 |archive-date = 29 July 2013 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130729010802/http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ySxeBl0C9g8 |url-status = live }} The season ended with a second consecutive UEFA Cup win, this time against fellow Spanish club [[RCD Espanyol|Espanyol]] at [[Hampden Park]], Glasgow.{{cite web |url = http://es.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/history/season=2006/index.html |title = El Sevilla revalidó su título |publisher = UEFA |access-date = 13 August 2010 |archive-date = 28 October 2010 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20101028072617/http://es.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/history/season=2006/index.html |url-status = dead }} The match went to penalties after finishing 2–2 after extra-time, with Sevilla goalkeeper [[Andrés Palop]] saving three of Espanyol's penalties.{{cite web|date=23 June 2007|title=El Sevilla cierra la mejor temporada de su historia con la Copa del Rey|url=http://archivo.marca.com/edicion/marca/futbol/copa_del_rey/previaxcronica/es/desarrollo/1009224.html|access-date=|website=Marca.com|archive-date=21 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210721012031/http://archivo.marca.com/edicion/marca/futbol/copa_del_rey/previaxcronica/es/desarrollo/1009224.html|url-status=live}} [[File:Sevilla Fútbol Club league performance 1929-present.svg|thumb|Chart of Sevilla FC league performance 1929–present]] On 12 November 2006, Sevilla played its 2,000th game in La Liga. Sevilla defeated [[Getafe CF|Getafe]] in the [[2007 Copa del Rey Final]], with Kanouté scoring the only goal in the game's 11th minute. Sevilla finished third in [[2006–07 La Liga|that season's La Liga]] to qualify for the [[2007–08 UEFA Champions League|2007–08 Champions League]], returning to the competition for the first time in 50 years. As a result of these successes, Sevilla was voted as the [[International Federation of Football History & Statistics|IFFHS]] Team of the Year for the second consecutive season, becoming the first club to achieve this.{{cite news |url= http://www.elpais.com/articulo/deportes/Sevilla/premio/IFFHS/mejor/equipo/pasado/ano/elpepudep/20070108elpepudep_11/Tes |title= El Sevilla, premio de la IFFHS al mejor equipo del pasado año |work= El País |date= 8 January 2007 |access-date= 1 December 2010 |archive-date= 7 March 2007 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070307193716/http://www.elpais.com/articulo/deportes/Sevilla/premio/IFFHS/mejor/equipo/pasado/ano/elpepudep/20070108elpepudep_11/Tes |url-status= live }} Sevilla won the [[2007 Supercopa de España]] against La Liga champions Real Madrid.{{cite web |url = http://www.cadenaser.com/articulo/deportes/Sevilla/vence/Real/Madrid/adjudica/Supercopa/csrcsrpor/20070819csrcsrdep_8/Tes/ |title = El Sevilla vence al Real Madrid y se adjudica la Supercopa |publisher = cadenaser.com |date = 19 August 2007 |access-date = 14 August 2010 |archive-date = 17 November 2011 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20111117033907/http://www.cadenaser.com/articulo/deportes/Sevilla/vence/Real/Madrid/adjudica/Supercopa/csrcsrpor/20070819csrcsrdep_8/Tes/ |url-status = dead }} The season started to derail, however, after defender [[Antonio Puerta]] suffered a heart attack in the first game of the season and died three days later on 28 August. Three days after his death, Sevilla then lost 3–1 to [[A.C. Milan|Milan]] in the [[2007 UEFA Super Cup]] in Monaco.{{cite web |url=http://www.uefa.com/uefasupercup/history/season=2007/index.html |title=2007: Milan overcome sombre Sevilla on UEFA.COM |website=[[UEFA]] |access-date=17 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100704113349/http://www.uefa.com/uefasupercup/history/season=2007/index.html |archive-date=4 July 2010 |url-status=dead}} Juande Ramos, the individual largely responsible for Sevilla's recent successes, resigned as manager on 27 October to take the post with [[Tottenham Hotspur F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]]; he was replaced by [[Sevilla Atlético]] manager [[Manuel Jiménez Jiménez|Manolo Jiménez]].{{cite news | url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/teams/t/tottenham_hotspur/7064928.stm | work=BBC News | title=Tottenham make Ramos head coach | date=27 October 2007 | access-date=22 September 2012 | archive-date=28 October 2007 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071028015424/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/t/tottenham_hotspur/7064928.stm | url-status=live }} In spite of the personnel issues, Sevilla nonetheless advanced in first place in its Champions League group ahead of [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] before later being eliminated in the round of 16 via penalties to [[Fenerbahçe S.K. (football)|Fenerbahçe]] of Turkey. [[File:Plantilla sevilla2.jpg|thumb|The squad in 2010]] In the summer of 2008, before Jiménez's debut season as first-team manager, [[Dani Alves]] and [[Seydou Keita]] were both sold to Barcelona, while [[Christian Poulsen]] left for [[Juventus FC|Juventus]]. Sevilla finished third in La Liga with a club record-equalling 21 victories and a club record number of away victories. The [[2009–10 La Liga|2009–10 season]] saw a third-consecutive qualification to the Champions League. On 19 May 2010, Sevilla defeated Atlético Madrid 2–0 in the [[2010 Copa del Rey Final]] at [[Camp Nou]], with goals from [[Diego Capel]] and [[Jesús Navas]].{{cite web |url = http://www.diariodesevilla.es/article/deportes/705797/una/copa/pura/ley.html |title = Una Copa de pura ley |publisher = Periódico Diario de Sevilla |date = 20 May 2010 |access-date = 14 August 2010 |archive-date = 25 May 2010 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100525045506/http://www.diariodesevilla.es/article/deportes/705797/una/copa/pura/ley.html |url-status = live }}{{cite web |url = http://www.marca.com/2010/05/19/futbol/copa_rey/1274306246.html?a=PROC1ea85621d8b9a9620e22dd285d069ec3&t=1282498647 |title = Navas, Capel, Zokora y Kanouté decantaron la final |work = Marca (newspaper) |date = 19 May 2010 |access-date = 21 August 2010 |archive-date = 17 July 2011 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110717155357/http://www.marca.com/2010/05/19/futbol/copa_rey/1274306246.html?a=PROC1ea85621d8b9a9620e22dd285d069ec3&t=1282498647 |url-status = live }} Before the 2010–11 season started, Sevilla lost to Barcelona 5–3 on aggregate in the [[2010 Supercopa de España|Supercopa]] and were eliminated in the [[2010–11 UEFA Champions League qualifying phase and play-off round|Champions League playoffs]] by Portuguese club [[S.C. Braga|Braga]].{{cite web|date=24 August 2010|title=Lima hat-trick ensures history for Braga|url=https://www.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/news/01e8-0e753a36fec3-68601b00eab6-1000--lima-hat-trick-ensures-history-for-braga/|access-date=|website=[[UEFA]]|language=en|archive-date=3 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220103034255/https://www.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/news/01e8-0e753a36fec3-68601b00eab6-1000--lima-hat-trick-ensures-history-for-braga/|url-status=live}} ===Unai Emery era=== [[File:Deporsevilla.jpg|thumb|[[Deportivo de La Coruña]] vs. Sevilla FC.]] On 14 January of the following year, after a 0–2 away loss to Valencia that left the Andalusians in 12th place, Jiménez was relieved of his duties, and was replaced by Spanish manager [[Unai Emery]]. The club went through an organizational financial crisis and was forced to sell team stars [[Álvaro Negredo]] and Jesús Navas, transactions that gave the club a combined €40 million; the duo was replaced by a contingent of younger players including strikers [[Carlos Bacca]] and [[Kevin Gameiro]].{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/0/football/27375727|title=Sevilla 0–0 Benfica (AET, 4–2 on pens)|date=14 May 2014|work=BBC Sport|access-date=15 May 2014|archive-date=14 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140514230151/http://www.bbc.com/sport/0/football/27375727|url-status=live}} On 14 May 2014, Sevilla defeated [[S.L. Benfica|Benfica]] on penalties in the [[2014 UEFA Europa League Final]] to claim their third triumph in the competition. After this season key midfielder [[Ivan Rakitić]] was sold to Barcelona for around €16 million (the deal was closed on 16 June 2014{{Cite news|date=16 June 2014|title=Ivan Rakitic: Barcelona sign Croatia midfielder from Sevilla|language=en-GB|work=BBC|url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/football/27879001|access-date=2019-10-12|archive-date=27 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027183126/https://www.bbc.com/sport/football/27879001|url-status=live}}). In summer 2015 top scorer Carlos Bacca, who had only joined two years previous, moved to Milan for €30 million.{{cite web|date=27 June 2015|title=Bacca se va al Milan|url=https://www.marca.com/2015/06/27/futbol/equipos/sevilla/1435432224.html|access-date=2019-10-12|website=MARCA.com|language=es|archive-date=12 October 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191012221956/https://www.marca.com/2015/06/27/futbol/equipos/sevilla/1435432224.html|url-status=live}} Despite these exits, the club acquired players [[Grzegorz Krychowiak]] and [[Éver Banega]] to reinforce the squad. On 27 May 2015, Sevilla were again Europa League champions after defeating Ukrainian club [[FC Dnipro Dnipropetrovsk|Dnipro Dnipropetrovsk]] 3–2 in the [[2015 UEFA Europa League Final|2015 Final]].{{cite web|title=Europa League – Sevilla break Dnipro hearts to defend title|url=https://uk.eurosport.yahoo.com/news/europa-league-dnipro-v-sevilla-europa-league-final-081415739--sow.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150528020122/https://uk.eurosport.yahoo.com/news/europa-league-dnipro-v-sevilla-europa-league-final-081415739--sow.html|archive-date=28 May 2015}} The goals for Sevilla were scored by [[Grzegorz Krychowiak]] and a brace from [[Carlos Bacca]].{{cite web|url=https://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/match/2015228--dnipro-vs-sevilla/|title=Dnipro-Sevilla 2015 History|website=[[UEFA]]|language=en|access-date=2019-10-12|archive-date=29 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929042717/https://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/season=2015/matches/round=2000592/match=2015228/|url-status=live}} By defeating Dnipro, they became the only club to have won the Europa League four times.{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2015/may/27/dnipro-dnipropetrovsk-sevilla-europa-league-final-match-report|title=Carlos Bacca double breaks Dnipro hearts for Sevilla to make history|date=28 May 2015|work=The Guardian|access-date=28 May 2015|archive-date=28 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150528001044/http://www.theguardian.com/football/2015/may/27/dnipro-dnipropetrovsk-sevilla-europa-league-final-match-report|url-status=live}} The club returned to the Europa League final for a third consecutive time, facing [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] in the [[2016 UEFA Europa League Final|2016 Final]]. After being down 0–1 at half-time, Sevilla bounced back in the second half to eventually win 3–1, with one goal scored from Kevin Gameiro and two from club captain [[Coke (footballer)|Coke]]. With its third consecutive Europa League title, Sevilla improved its record of most Europa League titles won, having lifted the trophy five times in the span of ten years.{{cite web|date=18 May 2016|title=Sevilla make it three in a row at Liverpool's expense|url=https://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/news/0250-0c51138a700a-9c0eb3116927-1000--sevilla-make-it-three-in-row-at-liverpool-s-expense/|website=[[UEFA]]|access-date=18 May 2016|archive-date=3 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171203223915/http://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/season=2016/matches/round=2000663/match=2017222/postmatch/report/index.html#sevilla+make+three+liverpools+expense--sow.html|url-status=live}} ===Post-Emery era=== Despite Sevilla's continued success in the Europa League, the [[2015–16 La Liga|2015–16 season]] proved to be another finish outside the top four, the side finishing in seventh. In response, Castro decided to engineer a resurrection of the club. The president is supported by a general director sometimes and a sports director. Throughout its history, Sevilla has had 28 presidents,{{cite web|title=Presidentes {{!}} Sevilla FC|url=https://sevillafc.es/el-club/historia/presidentes|access-date=2021-11-09|website=sevillafc.es|archive-date=9 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211109170324/https://sevillafc.es/el-club/historia/presidentes|url-status=live}} the first being [[Edward Farquharson Johnston]], a Scotsman. Those who have occupied the presidency for the longest periods have been Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán, Eugenio Montes Cabezas, José María del Nido Benavente, Luis Cuervas Vilches and José Castro Carmona. In 1992, Sevilla FC became a Sporting Limited Association, following the entry into force of the law that regulated this kind of sporting companies, and therefore the system of election of the president was amended from being elected by the members to be elected by the shareholders of the club. ===Ownership=== * Sevillistas de Nervion S.A. The lyrics were written by Ángel Luis Osquiguilea de Roncales and the music was composed by Manuel Osquiguilea de Roncales. * '''Centennial Anthem of Sevilla FC:''' Composed in 2005 by singer Javier Labandón 'El Arrebato' to commemorate the centenary of the registration of the club's articles of association, it became Spain's number one single and the best-selling anthem of a football club in the entire history of Spanish football, reaching the 2nd position of the best-selling albums in 2006.{{cite web |url = http://jenesaispop.com/2007/01/17/discos-vendidos-espana-2006/ |title = Discos más vendidos en España en 2006 |publisher = jenesaispop.com |date = 17 January 2007 |access-date = 1 August 2010 |archive-date = 17 September 2009 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090917181606/http://jenesaispop.com/2007/01/17/discos-vendidos-espana-2006/ |url-status = live }} On 9 October 2006, in the Estadio Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán, 'El Arrebato' was awarded the golden record his anthem. ===Crest=== From its foundation, the team used a double-circled crest. On the exterior circle, the name of the club and the date of its foundation were written, while in the interior circle on a white background the letters "SFC" were interlaced as they are on the current crest.{{Cite web |date=22 January 2024 |title=Behind the crest: Unraveling the history of Sevilla's crest - tacklefrombehind.com |url=https://tacklefrombehind.com/history-behind-sevilla-fc-logo/ |access-date=2024-01-27 |website=tacklefrombehind.com |language=en-GB}} This first crest was designed by Juan Lafita, who was a close associate of the club and was the son of the Sevillian painter José Lafita y Blanco. The second crest was designed in 1922 by Pablo Rodríguez Blanco, a draftsman of the Water Company. He divided the shield in three parts and together they formed the silhouette of a heart. The three figures that appear are the Christian saints portrayed on the coat of arms of the city – [[Isidore of Seville]], [[Ferdinand III of Castile]] and [[Leander of Seville]]. On the right side appear the initials "SFC," which were on the official shield from 1905 to 1922.{{cite web |url = http://www.sevillafc.es/_www/club.php |title = Escudo del Sevilla |publisher = sevillafc.es.club |access-date = 15 August 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100823040644/http://www.sevillafc.es/_www/club.php |archive-date = 23 August 2010}} Where the three parts meet, a football of the era appears. Regarding the red and white stripes, there are various theories, but it seems that the most coherent is that from the first time, the club wished that the official kit would be red and white. Another version indicates that the lower part is inspired on the flag which King [[Ferdinand III of Castile]] carried in the reconquest of Seville in 1248. ===Flag=== The definition of Sevilla's flag is in the articles of association of 1982, which is a modification of the old ones which were formed and deposited in the Record of Associations and Sports Federations of the Higher Council of Sports. Its title 1, article 6 states that this is a distinctive emblem of the club: :The flag, which will be rectangular, divided by a diagonal line that goes from the lower left angle to the upper right angle, which divides it into two triangles, the superior is white and the inferior red. ===Kit=== Sevilla wore shirts with a sponsor logo for the first time in the [[1986–87 La Liga|1986–87 season]], to promote the [[Seville Expo '92]]. Previously, before the 1980–81 season, the club signed its first kit-manufacturer deal with the German firm [[Adidas]]. From 2022 to 2025 the kit was manufactured by [[Castore (brand)|Castore]]. |publisher = sevillafc.com |access-date = 28 July 2010 }} The [[Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán Stadium]] was first planned in 1937 when the land was bought near to the then-home of Sevilla, in [[Nervión, Seville|Nervión]], and construction began in 1954. A contest was held for its design, won by the architect Manuel Muñoz Monasterio, who had also designed the home of Real Madrid, the [[Santiago Bernabéu Stadium]]. The construction of the stadium was completed in the summer of 1958 and was inaugurated on 7 September of the same year with a friendly match against [[Real Jaén]]. The east and west grandstands to the stadium were finished in 1974 under the presidency of Eugenio Montes Cabezas and increased the stadium's capacity to 70,000. For the 1982 World Cup, capacity was reduced from 70,000 to 66,000, and things were added like new lighting, the visor, and the mosaic on the main façade (by Santiago del Campo). The stadium held two World Cup games; a group match between the [[Soviet Union national football team|Soviet Union]] and [[Brazil national football team|Brazil]], as well as a semi-final between [[France national football team|France]] and [[Germany national football team|West Germany]].{{cite web |url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-09FMZCc-rI |title = Resumen partido Alemania Federal-Francia Mundial-82 |publisher = YouTube |access-date = 12 February 2010 |archive-date = 6 June 2016 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160606042057/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-09FMZCc-rI |url-status = live }} The [[1986 European Cup Final]] was held in the stadium, and won by [[FC Steaua București|Steaua București]] against Barcelona.{{cite web |url = http://videos.apnicommunity.com/Video,%20Item,1084703430.html |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20191215145315/http://videos.apnicommunity.com/Video,%2520Item,1084703430.html |url-status = dead |archive-date = 15 December 2019 |title = Noches de Copa Final 1985–86.avi |publisher = videos.apnicommunity.com |access-date = 12 August 2010 }} The capacity of the stadium was reduced to approximately 60,000. The last big modification was made during the mid-1990s, when according to [[FIFA]] rules, all standing areas had to be redeveloped into seating, reducing the capacity to the present 42,714. The [[Spain men's national football team|Spain national team]] have played 26 matches in the stadium since 1961, unbeaten with 21 wins and 5 draws.{{cite web |url=http://eu-football.info/_venue.php?id=812 |title=Football venue Estadio Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán, Seville |website=eu-football.info |access-date=2 October 2021 |archive-date=21 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150421154900/http://eu-football.info/_venue.php?id=812 |url-status=live }} To mark the club's centenary in 2005, an allegorical mosaic designed by Ben Yessef was built above the southern gate, depicting the history of the city of Seville. Above it, the club's badge floated in the wind.{{cite web |url = http://www.sevillafc.es/_www/club.php?op=esta |title = Estadio Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán |publisher = sevillafc.es |access-date = 28 July 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100630134432/http://www.sevillafc.es/_www/club.php?op=esta |archive-date = 30 June 2010}} The stadium currently houses the headquarters of the club's media, as well as an official store, club museum and trophy cabinet. ===Training facilities=== The sporting facilities known as La Ciudad Deportiva (The Sporting City) are used by the first team for training and by the reserve teams and women for matches. These facilities were inaugurated in 1974 and are located on the outskirts of the city on the road to [[Utrera]]. It has four natural grass pitches and three artificial pitches, as well as an artificial pitch for the Antonio Puerta Football School, changing rooms, gymnasium, press room, cafeteria, medical center and a recovering room.{{cite web |url = http://www.sevillafc.es/_www/club.php?op=ciu |title = Ciudad Deportiva José Ramón Cisneros Palacios |publisher = sevillafc.es |access-date = 14 August 2010 Graduates from it to Sevilla's first team include [[Sergio Ramos]] and [[Jesús Navas]], members of the Spain squad which won the [[2010 FIFA World Cup|2010 World Cup]] and [[UEFA Euro 2012]]. [[Sevilla FC C]], founded in 2003, compete in the fourth tier of Spanish football, the [[Tercera División]], having risen with four consecutive promotions from provincial and regional leagues. [[Sevilla FC (women)|Sevilla's women's team]] play in the top-flight of Spanish women's football, the [[Super Liga Femenil de Fútbol|Super Liga]], and currently play their home games at the club's training ground, [[Ciudad Deportiva José Ramón Cisneros Palacios]]. Sevilla acquired the women's club from CD Hispalis in 2004, and the club had its greatest success in the 2005–06 season, when it came runner-up in the Super Liga and the [[Copa de la Reina de Fútbol|national cup]]. Since its foundation for the 2007–08 season, the Spanish indoor football league has included a Sevilla veterans' team. [[Sevilla FC Puerto Rico]], of [[Juncos, Puerto Rico|Juncos]], is a Puerto Rican football club of the [[Puerto Rico Soccer League]]. The side affiliated to Sevilla in 2008, and share a similar badge and kit. Since 2008, Sevilla has been one of two Spanish clubs (the other being [[Atlético Madrid]], to compete in [[Superleague Formula]], in which cars endorsed by professional football clubs compete in races across the world. The [[Regata Sevilla-Betis|Sevilla-Betis regatta]] is an annual [[rowing (sport)|rowing]] competition in Seville's [[Guadalquivir]] river, held since 1960. Different categories of boats represent Sevilla and its cross-city rival [[Real Betis]]. Sevilla have won on 30 of the 47 regattas. ==Support== ===Fans=== Since Sevilla became Sporting Limited Association, the concept of membership disappeared. Only the shareholders can take part in the decisions of the club according to the percentage of the capital they hold. The minority shareholders of the club are organised in a federation that represents them in the General Meeting of Shareholders that the club celebrates every year. People who are traditionally referred to as members are currently fans who purchase a yearly season ticket which allows them to attend all home matches that season. Sometimes these members enjoy some specific advantages over the rest of the fans. ===Fan clubs=== Sevilla's fan clubs are mainly concentrated in the city of Seville, [[Seville (province)|its province]] and the rest of Andalusia. The presence of fan clubs in other autonomous communities is greater in [[Catalonia]] and [[Extremadura]]. Most of them are integrated into the "San Fernando Fan Clubs Federation" (Federación de Peñas Sevillistas "San Fernando"), which, according to its statutes, is totally independent from the directive board of the club, having its own board and not being intervened. ===Ultras=== [[File:Estadio Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán Gol Norte tifo-2007-04-05.jpg|thumb|Biris Norte's banner at the Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán Stadium]] The Biris Norte is an organized group of [[Ultras|ultra]] supporters located in the North grandstand of the Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán. The group's name comes from the Gambian player Alhaji Momodo Njie, nicknamed [[Biri Biri]], who became very popular among the Sevilla fans in the 1970s. The "Biris Norte" was created in the 1974–75 season and is one of the oldest groups of Ultra fans in Spain. ===Rivalries=== {{See also|Seville derby}} Sevilla compete in the [[Seville derby]] against their cross-city rivals [[Real Betis]]. The two played each other for the first time on 8 October 1915 in a match which was won 4–3 by Sevilla. The game is considered one of the most important [[Spanish football rivalries|derbies in Spanish football]].
